Regulation · IT security · SMEs

NIS2 for small IT companies and freelancers: thresholds, deadlines, duties

The German NIS2 implementation act has been in force since 6 December 2025. Whether a company is directly affected depends on sector and size – but small firms feel it as suppliers too.

Serge Zabolotny · 2026-10-27

  • NIS2
  • IT-Sicherheit
  • BSI
  • Compliance
  • Backup
  • Lieferkette

The key facts

TopicAccording to the source
In force6 December 2025 (promulgated 5 December 2025, BGBl. I No. 301)
Particularly important entitiesfrom 250 employees, or turnover above €50 million and balance sheet above €43 million
Important entitiesfrom 50 employees, or turnover and balance sheet each above €10 million
Extra conditionmembership of a sector listed in Annex 1 or 2
BSI registrationwithin three months; for entities already covered by 6 March 2026
Reports for significant incidentsearly warning 24 hours, notification 72 hours, final report no later than one month after
Finesup to €10 million (particularly important) or €7 million (important entities)

Important: size alone does not decide. Only the combination of a threshold and a sector makes a company a regulated entity. When unsure, the BSI’s self-assessment helps – and, if in doubt, legal advice.

And if I am below the thresholds?

A freelancer or micro-company is usually below 50 employees and therefore not directly affected – that is my reading of the thresholds, not legal advice. NIS2 still becomes noticeable through the supply chain: affected customers have to keep an eye on risks at their service providers and will ask for evidence, for example on access control, backups and incident handling. A commentary on the draft bill (usd, 2024) explicitly lists supply-chain security, vulnerability handling, backup and business continuity, access control and multi-factor authentication among the measures; whether the final wording says the same should be checked in the law.

Practical evidence worth having anyway

  • Backups with a tested restore: see backup the 3-2-1 way and the restore test.
  • Access control and multi-factor login: how I do it in the homelab, see zero trust for the homelab.
  • Traceable delivery: a documented CI/CD pipeline shows how changes reach production.
  • A plan for security incidents: who is informed when? Closely related to the CRA reporting duty.

Sources and limits

  • ADVISORI: NIS2 implementation act (consultancy blog; entry into force, thresholds, deadlines, fines)
  • usd: NIS-2, the key points (commentary on the 2024 draft, used only for the list of measures)
  • The Federal Law Gazette is binding; neither source is an official text.

Not legal advice. I am a developer, not a lawyer. The details come from the sources listed (as of October 2026); the legal text is what counts.
